<reason>Both sides argued well, but A built the more resilient case. A's opening grounded its claim in a well-known, plausible mechanism (transition-related health/safety spikes) and a real historical data point (the 1970s US repeal of permanent DST), then successfully pivoted when B's sharp early reframe ("winter already runs on standard time under switching") neutralized A's dark-morning argument. A's pivot to "the switch achieves the same winter outcome as my plan, but adds a mandatory, physiologically disruptive jolt twice a year" kept a live, coherent throughline: mandatory forced harm vs. an early sunrise that is merely wasted, not harmful. B never rebutted the transition-cost mechanism with more than assertion ("shiftable," "sleep debt reducible by anticipation"), and B's most promising counter-punch — that America's 1970s reversal reveals a preference for switching, not standard time — was cut off by the word-limit clip before it landed, an execution cost that fell on B twice across the debate versus once for A. B's coordination-problem argument against decentralized institutional flexibility was genuinely strong and exposed a real weakness in A's Q&A answer, but it wasn't enough to overturn A's cleaner mandatory-harm-vs-mere-inconvenience framing, which both closings ultimately circled around, with A's version landing slightly more decisively given the unrebutted asymmetry claim.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's opening rebuttal move — pointing out that A's entire dark-winter-morning case is already satisfied by the existing switch, so it argues for switching rather than against it — was the single most reframing-heavy exchange; A's answer (the switch still imposes a discrete transition cost with no historical parallel for standard time in summer) is what let A recover the debate rather than lose it outright.</best_rebuttal>
